articles.title: 'They were legends': Humpback whales make spectacular comeback off Brazil's coast
articles.summary: Once driven to the brink of extinction, humpback whales have thrived in the South Atlantic since a worldwide moratorium on commercial whaling came into force in 1986, offering a bonanza to scientists who come each year to Brazil's Abrolhos archipelago to record and study the cetaceans.
articles.content:
Female humpback whales off the coast of Brazil now have their pick of mates, who slap the water with their tails and jostle for attention – a scene that would have been unthinkable a few decades ago.

Driven to near-extinction in the 1980s, there are now about 35,000 humpback whales in the South Atlantic, almost half of the world's total.

The warm waters off the coast of Brazil are the largest breeding ground for Southern Atlantic humpbacks. Males compete for the chance to mate, and females give birth and nurse their calves.

They also offer a bonanza to scientists who come each year to the Abrolhos archipelago off the coast of the state of Bahia to record and study hundreds of the cetaceans.

Four decades ago, no one even knew there were whales in Brazil, said Enrico Marcovaldi, founder of the Humpback Whale Institute (IBJ) – one of Brazil's leading organisations researching and protecting the species.

The first time he saw one, he mistook it for a rock.

"They were legends. We had never seen one," Marcovaldi told AFP.

Wearing a life jacket and helmet, and armed with a crossbow, biologist Fabio Fontes pursues the group of males in a small boat who are competing to mate with a female © Evaristo Sa, AFP

Humpback populations have thrived since a worldwide moratorium on commercial whaling in 1986.

The following year, Brazil banned the practice by law and later declared the Abrolhos breeding grounds a protected area.

In 2014, the humpback whale was removed from Brazil's list of threatened species, and its population has continued to thrive ever since.

Family ties

Wearing a life jacket and helmet, and armed with a crossbow, biologist Fabio Fontes pursues a group of males who are competing to mate with a female.

From his small boat, he fires an arrow that pierces the back of one whale before dropping into the water. He retrieves it with a sample of skin and blubber attached.

A team of scientists and journalists, including AFP, follows Fontes's moves from a catamaran.

A pattern of white markings against the black of a humpback's tail is its fingerprint -- a unique pattern that allows researchers to identify individual whales from photographs © Evaristo Sa, AFP

Milton Marcondes, the IBJ's research coordinator, explained that the samples can be used to establish family ties between the whales, known for one of the longest migrations of any mammal on the planet.

Years ago, the researchers discovered that a humpback born in Abrolhos was related to another spotted off South Georgia, a remote island some 4,000 kilometres (2500 miles) to the south.

The finding helped establish the migration route of the animals, which can reach up to 16 metres (roughly 50 feet) long as adults and weigh as much as six elephants.

AI identification

A pattern of white markings against the black of a humpback's tail is its fingerprint – a unique pattern that allows researchers to identify individual whales from photographs.

The comparison, which once required many pairs of eyes and hours of work, can now be done in seconds by Happy Whale, an artificial intelligence platform that has already identified 8,300 Brazilian humpbacks.

The tool helped uncover a world record: one humpback identified in Brazil was spotted more than 15,000 kilometres away off Australia's east coast, according to research published in May.

Milton Marcondes, the research coordinator at Brazil's Humpback Whale Institute, processes samples from a humpback whale. © Evaristo Sa, AFP

"We are seeing that populations in the Southern Hemisphere are much more interconnected than we imagined," Marcondes told AFP.

These days, the whales face threats from maritime traffic, fishing nets, and warming seas caused by climate change, which threatens the krill they survive on.

The IBJ has received financial support from Brazil's state oil company Petrobras for 30 years.

Petrobras, which drills for oil off Brazil and recently made new discoveries off the coast of the Amazon, supports several species recovery projects in the country.

In October, the Abrolhos archipelago was designated a "Hope Spot" by Mission Blue, founded by oceanographer Sylvia Earle, recognising its rich biodiversity and importance to marine conservation.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
articles.reasoning: The article reports the significant recovery of humpback whale populations off Brazil's coast following a global ban on commercial whaling and national protections, highlighting a major conservation success with broad environmental and scientific impact. It details the species' comeback, ongoing research efforts including AI identification, and the designation of the breeding grounds as a protected Hope Spot, all demonstrating substantial positive real-world impact and meaningful scope.
articles.personality_title: Humpback whales make a strong comeback off Brazil’s coast
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Humpback whales in the South Atlantic were almost wiped out by hunting by the 1980s. In 1986, a worldwide ban on commercial whaling helped protect them, and Brazil later created laws to stop hunting and protect whale breeding areas.

**What happened** – Since the ban, the humpback whale population off Brazil’s coast has grown to about 35,000, nearly half of all humpbacks worldwide. Scientists study these whales each year at the Abrolhos archipelago, Brazil’s largest breeding ground. Researchers use special tools like crossbows to collect small skin samples and artificial intelligence to identify individual whales by the unique patterns on their tails.

**Impact** – This recovery is important because it shows how protection laws can help endangered animals return. The whales’ return also helps scientists learn about their long migration routes and family ties. The area where they breed was recently named a “Hope Spot” to highlight its importance for ocean life. This success story is a clear example of how nature can heal when given a chance.

**What’s next step** – Scientists will continue to monitor the whales using AI and tracking methods to better understand their behavior and migration. Conservation efforts will keep protecting their habitat from threats like fishing nets, ship traffic, and climate change. The work supported by organizations and companies aims to ensure these whales thrive for many years to come.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Thanks to global and local protections, humpback whales have made a remarkable recovery off Brazil’s coast, becoming a key focus for science and conservation.

articles.title: Australia’s red soil may be hiding a massive clean energy source
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered that Western Australia’s iron-rich rocks can naturally generate hydrogen and that the process may be boosted to produce much larger amounts. If it can be scaled up, the vast formations beneath the Pilbara could become a major new source of low-emission energy for Australia and potentially the world.
articles.content:
Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have identified a potentially important source of low-emission energy beneath Western Australia, where vast iron-rich formations may be capable of generating naturally occurring hydrogen.

The findings suggest that the region's geology could eventually support a new domestic energy source and, if developed at scale, a major hydrogen export industry.

Magnetite Could Generate Hydrogen Underground

The research focuses on magnetite, a mineral that is abundant in Western Australia's huge iron ore deposits across the Pilbara region.

Scientists from ECU's School of Engineering found that magnetite can release hydrogen gas when it reacts with hot water under conditions similar to those deep below the Earth's surface.

The team also discovered a way to stimulate the process. By injecting a solution into banded iron formations, the researchers were able to increase hydrogen generation, raising the possibility that naturally produced hydrogen could one day be deliberately enhanced underground.

"Australia could be sitting on a massive, untapped energy reserve -- and the potential is enormous," Associate Professor Alireza Keshavarz said.

"There is enough hydrogen for Australia to benefit for generations, and potentially enough for us to become a major exporter of clean energy to the rest of the world."

Recreating Deep Underground Conditions

To investigate how the process works, the researchers placed magnetite samples in water at 200°C under high pressure for 60 days. Those conditions were designed to reproduce the hot, pressurized environment found deep underground.

The experiments gave researchers a clearer picture of how natural hydrogen can form within rock and what conditions are needed for production to continue over time.

The findings are especially significant for Western Australia because the region contains some of the largest banded iron formations on Earth.

"Western Australia has some of the world's largest banded iron formations. If we can unlock this resource at scale, it could be transformative for our energy future," lead author Kaveh Moghanirahimi said.

"We even see the potential for Western Australia to strengthen its energy independence during times of crisis through access to this naturally generated hydrogen."

From Laboratory Experiments to Natural Hydrogen Exploration

Professor Stefan Iglauer, from ECU's School of Engineering, said the results bring researchers closer to understanding how hydrogen production might work in real underground rock formations rather than only in controlled laboratory settings.

"This work helps bridge the gap between laboratory experiments and real geological systems," Professor Iglauer said.

The study also found that the amount of magnetite alone does not determine how much hydrogen can be produced. The structure of the rock matters as well, particularly whether water can move through it and reach fresh mineral surfaces.

"Our findings show that hydrogen production depends not only on the amount of magnetite present, but also on how easily water can access fresh mineral surfaces through fractures, pores and permeable pathways."

That means fractures, pores, and other pathways through the rock could play a critical role in determining whether natural hydrogen can be generated efficiently enough to become a practical energy resource.

The research, Geometry-driven controls on hydrothermal natural hydrogen generation from magnetite mineral, has been published in the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy.

articles.title: The Forested Floodplains of Congaree National Park
articles.summary: The meandering Congaree River sustains towering forest ecosystems and fashions oxbow lakes as it shifts across its floodplain.
articles.content:
The OLI on Landsat 9 captured this image of the Congaree River winding through floodplain forests in Congaree National Park on August 18, 2025. NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison

Among the 63 U.S. national parks, few are as defined by a single river's floodplain as Congaree National Park in South Carolina. While the features are also prominent in other parks, a full 80 percent of Congaree National Park lies within the Congaree River floodplain.

It's a place home to one of the largest intact tracts of old-growth bottomland hardwood forests in the United States. In this image captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9, the river winds through the forested plain, along with curving bands of green that trace old channels, ridges, and swales left behind as the river gradually migrated across it. Slight differences in elevation in these paleochannels and other landforms affect how frequently they flood, producing distinct ecosystems that appear in contrasting shades of green.

The river flows through flat, soft terrain, which encourages the formation of bends and meanders. Water typically flows faster on the outside of bends, leading to more rapid erosion as the channel carves into the outer riverbank. It moves more slowly on the inside of bends, resulting in the deposition of sediment and the growth of sandy features called point bars. Over time, this process can cut off a bend from the main river channel, forming U-shaped oxbow lakes.

The National Park Service lists Weston Lake, 1.2 miles (1.9 kilometers) from the visitor center, as one of the park’s most permanent oxbow lakes, noting that it is relatively deep and lacks the shallow clay and silt layer found in most of the park's other oxbow lakes, such as Devil's Elbow. On the right side of the image is Bates Old River, a roughly 4-mile-long abandoned channel of the Congaree River and one of the longest oxbow lakes in South Carolina. Over time, abandoned channels and oxbow lakes can fill with sediment and become shallow wetlands. Some of these low-lying, water-filled features are known as sloughs, where flood-tolerant cypress-tupelo forests tend to grow.

While loggers targeted forests along the Congaree in the 1880s, challenges such as frequent flooding, interminably muddy roads, and mosquito-plagued conditions meant that most of the floodplain forests escaped the widespread logging that transformed other parts of the Southeast. By the 1950s, conservationists had begun to recognize how rare old-growth forests of this type had become in the region. Congress designated the area a national monument in 1976, and it became a national park in 2003.

As the river snakes its way through the park's mostly flat terrain, it overflows its banks several times per year, usually in the winter and early spring but also in the summer and fall after hurricanes and major rainstorms. These floods distribute broad layers of nutrient-rich silt throughout the floodplain, nourishing the forests and contributing to the high concentration of unusually large trees in the park.

Over the decades, Congaree National Park has harbored a remarkable array of giant "champion" trees that have held national and state size records for their species. Though individual trees have gained and lost champion status as they have been damaged, have died, or been surpassed by newly measured trees elsewhere, Congaree trees such as the possumhaw (Ilex decidua), water hickory (Carya aquatica), loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), laurel oak (Quercus laurifolia), swamp tupelo (Nyssa biflora), and sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua) have held records at times.

During this National Park Week, celebrate by exploring Earth Observatory's U.S. National Parks from Space collection. You can also check out the offerings of Earth to Sky, a collaborative program that connects NASA science with park service rangers across the nation.

NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Adam Voiland.

Downloads August 18, 2025

articles.personality_title: How the Congaree River Shapes a Rare Forest in South Carolina
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Congaree National Park in South Carolina is mostly made up of a floodplain, a flat area that the Congaree River flows through and floods regularly. This park protects one of the largest old forests that grow in wet, low-lying land in the United States.

**What happened** – On August 18, 2025, a satellite called Landsat 9 took a detailed picture showing how the Congaree River twists through the park’s forest and floodplain. The river’s bends create special land shapes like oxbow lakes—U-shaped lakes formed when a river changes course—and these areas support different types of plants and trees.

**Impact** – This park is important because it has rare, untouched forests that survived logging in the 1800s due to difficult conditions like flooding and muddy roads. The river’s floods bring nutrient-rich soil that helps giant trees grow. Some of these trees have been the biggest of their kind in the country. Protecting this area keeps these unique forests and their wildlife safe.

**What's next step** – The park continues to be studied and cared for by scientists and the National Park Service. Programs connect NASA science with park rangers to help people learn about the park from space and on the ground. Visiting or following these efforts can teach us more about how rivers shape forests and how to protect them.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Congaree River’s natural floods help maintain one of the rarest and biggest old-growth floodplain forests in the U.S., making Congaree National Park a special place for nature and science.

articles.personality_title_es: Cómo el río Congaree moldea un bosque raro en Carolina del Sur
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El parque nacional Congaree en Carolina del Sur está formado en su mayoría por una llanura de inundación, un área plana por donde fluye y se desborda regularmente el río Congaree. Este parque protege uno de los bosques antiguos más grandes que crecen en tierras bajas y húmedas en Estados Unidos.

**Qué pasó** – El 18 de agosto de 2025, un satélite llamado Landsat 9 tomó una imagen detallada que muestra cómo el río Congaree serpentea a través del bosque y la llanura de inundación del parque. Las curvas del río crean formas especiales en el terreno, como lagos en forma de herradura, que se forman cuando un río cambia de curso y que albergan diferentes tipos de plantas y árboles.

**Impacto** – Este parque es importante porque tiene bosques raros e intactos que escaparon de la tala en el siglo XIX debido a condiciones difíciles como las inundaciones y caminos fangosos. Las inundaciones del río traen tierra rica en nutrientes que ayuda a crecer a árboles gigantes. Algunos de estos árboles han sido los más grandes de su especie en el país. Proteger este lugar mantiene seguros estos bosques únicos y su vida silvestre.

**Próximo paso** – El parque sigue siendo estudiado y cuidado por científicos y el Servicio de Parques Nacionales. Programas conectan la ciencia de la NASA con guardabosques para ayudar a la gente a aprender sobre el parque desde el espacio y en el lugar. Visitar o seguir estos esfuerzos puede enseñar más sobre cómo los ríos moldean los bosques y cómo protegerlos.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las inundaciones naturales del río Congaree ayudan a mantener uno de los bosques antiguos de llanura de inundación más raros y grandes de EE. UU., haciendo del parque nacional Congaree un lugar especial para la naturaleza y la ciencia.
